newsitem.title: USA: Clinton moving to build support for trade bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton moving to build support for trade bill.

text.p: President Clinton is stepping up efforts to build support in what is expected to be a tough fight for trade legislation needed to bring Chile into the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), White House officials said Wednesday.

The so-called fast track trade negotiation authority "will be an important element" in a major foreign policy speech President Clinton plans to make at a meeting of newspaper editors on Friday, officials said.
"The president will continue to express in a very clear way his commitment to achieve fast track authority," an official said.

Clinton is also expected to meet next week with leading members of Congress to talk about foreign policy issues and the trade legislation is expected to be a part of those discussions as well, officials said.

Clinton had mentioned the legislation when he set out his agenda for the year in his annual State of the Union address in January and Chilean President Eduardo Frei made a pitch for the legislation during a visit to Washington in February.

But the business community and free trade supporters in Congress want Clinton to play a bigger role in pushing for the authority, which is needed to negotiate trade agreements without fear they will be changed by lawmakers. Congress can either vote yes or no for trade agreements under fast track, but not amend them.

Supporters fear that, without a major push by Clinton, House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt and other opponents of NAFTA's expansion would gain the upper hand in the debate and the United States would lose out to the European Union and other global trade competitors interested in Latin American markets.

Fast track authority expired in 1994, and the administration needs it order to begin negotiations with Chile on its entry into NAFTA, the first step in creating a broader Free Trade of the Americas Agreement (FTAA) by 20005.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich expressed concern that the administration has yet to send Congress a proposed bill.
"We'd like to move it as quickly as possible," Gingrich, R-Georgia, told reporters at a meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien.
"We really want to pass this bill very rapidly."

Canadian officials during Chretien's visit this week, expressed their desire to see Washington move quickly on fast track. Canada has struck its own free trade deal with Chile, but officials said U.S. leadership is needed in the broader effort to establish a hemispheric free trade zone.
The White House does not want to send Congress proposed legislation until they worked out a compromise that will win both Democratic and Republican votes.
Gingrich and other Republicans, who generally have supported free trade agreements, want the administration to round up some support from its own Democrats.
"They (the administration) would have to get votes from Democrats," Gingrich said.
The main stumbling block has been a dispute between Republicans and Democrats over authority to negotiate labor and environmental issues in trade agreements.

Administration officials said they want a broad negotiating authority that will allow them to address those issues. Republicans, who control Congress, oppose including labor and environmental issues in trade negotiating authority.
A senior administration official said the two sides are still trying to work out a compromise.
